articles.author: Rasool Khan
articles.description:
At some point while preparing for interviews, something odd happens.
You solve a problem, move on, then a few days later you see another one that feels… familiar. Different story, different variables but the same underlying logic.
At first, it feels like a coincidence. But, it isn’t.

Most DSA problems aren’t truly new.
They’re variations.
Different constraints. Slight tweaks. New wording.
Two pointers.
Sliding windows.
Prefix sums.
Binary search.
A bit of hashing.
Once you notice that, it’s hard to unsee it.
A lot of us are taught to treat every problem as something unique.
Read carefully.
So when problems start repeating, it can feel like you’re “cheating” by reusing ideas like you’re not really learning.
That framing is what makes DSA feel harder than it needs to be.
In real systems, we…

If you've worked with React, you've probably used the Provider pattern. It's a component that wraps children and provides them with data via context.
:let directive combined with assign_async.
I had a product detail page that needed to show similar products. The naive approach would be to load them in the parent LiveView's mount:
def mount(params, _session, socket) do
  product = get_product!(params)

  # Blocking the mount with an async search operation 🙈
  {:ok, similar_products} = Search.similar_products(product.id, limit: 12)

  socket
  |> assign(:product, product)
  |> assign(:similar_products, similar_products)
  |> ok()
end

Two problems here:
Blocking mount - the search delays the entire page render
Scattered concerns - similar products logic lives in the parent LiveView
Instead,…
articles.title: Phoenix LiveComponent Provider Pattern
